title: Modules & Packages
summary: Reuse code across files with import, and understand where Python looks for it.

checkpoints.title: import brings code into your file
checkpoints.content: `import math` makes everything in the math module available as `math.something` — for example `math.sqrt(16)`. `from math import sqrt` instead pulls just that one name directly into your file, so you'd call it as `sqrt(16)` without the prefix.
checkpoints.explanation: A module is just a `.py` file full of reusable code; a package is a folder of modules. Both get pulled in with import — Python doesn't re-run the same module twice even if it's imported from multiple places.

hints.H0: import gives you access to a module's contents through a prefix.
hints.H1: from X import Y pulls just one name in directly, no prefix needed.
hints.H2: math.sqrt(16) and (after `from math import sqrt`) sqrt(16) do the same thing.

checkpoints.title: Predict the correct call
checkpoints.content: After `import random`, which call correctly gets a random integer between 1 and 6?

options.explanation: Plain `import random` requires the module prefix on every call to something inside it.
That would only work after `from random import randint` — a plain `import random` still requires the random. prefix.
Modules aren't accessed like dictionaries — use dot notation (module.name), not square-bracket indexing.

checkpoints.explanation: A plain `import module_name` always requires the dotted prefix (module_name.thing) to reach anything inside it.

hints.H0: Plain import keeps everything behind a prefix.
hints.H1: The prefix is the module's own name, followed by a dot.

checkpoints.title: Import with a shorter alias
checkpoints.content: Write an import statement that imports the datetime module under the shorter local name dt.
checkpoints.explanation: The `as` keyword after an import gives the module a different local name — dt.datetime.now() instead of the longer datetime.datetime.now().

hints.H0: There's a keyword that renames an import right where you write it.
hints.H1: It goes between the module name and the alias: import X as Y.

checkpoints.title: Predict a from-import's scope
checkpoints.content: After `from math import pi`, which of these works without raising a NameError?

options.explanation: `from math import pi` pulls the name pi directly into your file's namespace, so it's usable on its own.
The math module itself was never imported here — only the single name pi was, so math.pi raises a NameError for math.
Same issue — math itself isn't available, only the specific name pi that was imported from it.

checkpoints.explanation: `from X import Y` brings only Y into scope directly, not the module X itself — using X.anything afterward fails.

hints.H0: from-import is selective — it only brings in what you name.
hints.H1: The module's own name doesn't become available this way.
